text:
I went and leaned against the mantelpiece, directly opposite Marguerite, and watched her dance. No sooner had she noticed me than she became flustered. I saw it, and greeted her distractedly with a gesture of my hand and a glance.

When I thought that after the ball she would leave not with me, but with that rich fool, when I pictured to myself what would probably follow their return to her home, the blood rushed to my face, and I felt the urge to disrupt their lovemaking.

After the country dance, I went to pay my respects to the mistress of the house, who was displaying to the guests’ eyes magnificent shoulders and half of a dazzling bosom.

That woman was beautiful and, in terms of figure, more beautiful than Marguerite. I understood this even better from certain glances Marguerite cast at Olympe while I was speaking to her. The man who became this woman’s lover could be as proud as M. de N... was, and she was beautiful enough to inspire a passion equal to the one Marguerite had inspired in me.

She had no lover at that time. It would not be difficult to become one. All that was needed was to display enough gold to make her take notice.

My mind was made up. This woman would be my mistress.

I began playing the part of a suitor by dancing with Olympe.

Half an hour later, Marguerite, pale as a corpse, put on her fur-lined cloak and left the ball.




Chapter XXIV


That was something already, but it was not enough. I understood the power I had over this woman, and I abused it like a coward.

When I think that she is dead now, I wonder whether God will ever forgive me for the harm I did.

After supper, which was extremely boisterous, we began to gamble.

I sat down beside Olympe and staked my money with such boldness that she could not help noticing. In an instant, I won a hundred and fifty or two hundred louis, which I spread out before me and upon which she fixed ardent eyes.

I was the only person who was not wholly absorbed in the game and who paid attention to her. I went on winning for the rest of the night, and it was I who gave her money with which to play, for she had lost everything she had with her and probably everything she had at home.

At five in the morning, everyone left.

I had won three hundred louis.

All the gamblers were already downstairs; I alone had remained behind without anyone noticing, for I was not a friend of any of those gentlemen.

Olympe herself was lighting the staircase, and I was about to go down like the others when, turning back toward her, I said:

“I must speak to you.”

“Tomorrow,” she said to me.

“No, now.”

“What do you have to say to me?”

“You will see.”

And I went back into the apartment.

“You lost, didn’t you?” I said to her.

“Yes.”

“Everything you had at home?”

She hesitated.

“Be frank.”

“Well, it is true.”

“I have won three hundred louis. Here they are, if you are willing to keep me here.”

And at the same time, I threw the gold onto the table.

“And why this proposal?”

“Because I love you, by God!”

“No, but because you are in love with Marguerite and want to take revenge on her by becoming my lover. A woman like me is not so easily deceived, my dear friend; unfortunately, I am still too young and too beautiful to accept the role you are offering me.”

“So you refuse?”

“Yes.”

“Would you rather love me for nothing? In that case, I would be the one to refuse. Think it over, my dear Olympe. If I had sent some third party to offer you these three hundred louis on my behalf, on the conditions I attach to them, you would have accepted. I preferred to deal with you directly. Accept without trying to discover the reasons that make me act; tell yourself that you are beautiful, and that there is nothing surprising about my being in love with you.”

Marguerite was a kept woman like Olympe, and yet, the first time I saw her, I would never have dared say to her what I had just said to this woman. That was because I loved Marguerite, because I had discerned in her instincts that this other creature lacked, and because, at the very moment when I was proposing this bargain, despite her extreme beauty, the woman with whom I was about to conclude it disgusted me.

She ended by accepting, of course, and at noon I left her home as her lover; but I left her bed without carrying away any memory of the caresses and words of love she had believed herself obliged to lavish on me in return for the six thousand francs I left her.

And yet men had ruined themselves over that woman.

From that day onward, I subjected Marguerite to unremitting persecution. Olympe and she ceased seeing one another; you can easily understand why. I gave my new mistress a carriage and jewels, I gambled—in short, I committed every extravagance befitting a man in love with a woman like Olympe. Word of my new passion spread at once.

Even Prudence was taken in by it and ended by believing that I had completely forgotten Marguerite. Marguerite, whether she had guessed the motive behind my actions or was mistaken like the others, responded with great dignity to the wounds I inflicted on her every day. Only, she appeared to be suffering, for wherever I encountered her, each time I saw her she was paler and sadder than before. My love for her, exalted to such a pitch that it believed itself to have become hatred, rejoiced at the sight of this daily suffering. Several times, in circumstances in which I behaved with vile cruelty, Marguerite raised such pleading eyes to me that I blushed at the role I had assumed and came close to asking her forgiveness for it.

But these fits of repentance lasted no longer than a flash of lightning, and Olympe, who had ended by setting aside every kind of pride and had understood that by hurting Marguerite she would obtain from me whatever she wanted, constantly incited me against her and insulted her whenever she found an opportunity, with the persistent cowardice of a woman given license by a man.
